name: North Face
text: [overview] Get going early, since cornices can break from the summit ridge above.
[overview] Steep neve and WI3 for several pitches lead to a rock band, where two pitches of M4-5, and maybe one M6 move, follow.
[overview] Work left (east) when possible to get out from beneath the 40' cornices 800' above, then go 700' straight up more steep neve.
[approach] The face carries cornices on the summit ridge above, which is why parties start early.
earlierWhy: why: Steep neve and ice with cornices in winter; could not confirm the face carries no glacier.

name: Stella by Starlight
text: [overview] A serious mixed line up the Wheeler Peak headwall above the cirque: snow and ice to a ramp, wet rock beside a water gully, aid through dripping overhangs, then a long icy ramp trending left to exit just below the summit.
[detailed_rack] Bring snow and ice anchors, plus stoppers, hexes and thin pitons for rock.
earlierWhy: why: Wheeler's cirque holds a small glacier reported to have crevasses at the headwall, and the route starts on snow and ice there.

name: Full Richardson
text: [overview] Up a distinct couloir on the North Face: two WI2/3 steps and about 300 ft of moderate snow lead to the 30m crux, steep aerated ice with poor gear but great axe sticks, behaving more like alpine than water ice.
[overview] A picket above the curtain makes the belay;
[overview] Moderate snow in the bowl follows, around 600 feet to the summit;
[overview] Snow steepens under the summit block and may be loose at the very top;
[detailed_rack] Screws (with stubbies) and pickets.
[approach] Two short steps of ice or snow, depending on the season, come first, then moderate snow leads up the couloir.
[approach] Watch the snow stability here and check the avalanche forecast.
earlierWhy: why: North face couloir on a glaciated peak, but text never says whether a crevassed glacier is crossed.

name: Nine O'clock Gully
text: [overview] It needs deep snow to be in shape and might carry a cornice.
[descent_text] Either gully needs solid snow cover to be in condition, and a cornice may cap the top of this one, so look it over from below before committing.
earlierWhy: why: Winter snow gully needing deep cover; the text does not say whether a glacier is on the line.

name: West Rib
text: [overview] The lower ridge is moderate snow;
[overview] Protection is rarely needed until the pinnacle, so most parties carry a few pickets or screws for the snow and a light rack of nuts and slings for the top.
earlierWhy: why: A west-side ridge route with moderate snow lower down and no glacier crossing. | secondReview: unsure/yes: Moderate snow on the lower ridge of Jefferson; glacier contact not settled by any text.

name: Iron Maiden
text: [detailed_rack] Thin conditions call for pins and nuts, while fat ones may allow screws and an occasional picket.

name: North Milk Creek Glacier

name: Devil's Kitchen Headwall (DKH) - Left Variation
text: [detailed_rack] With fat ice and consolidated snow above, take pickets and medium-length screws.

[approach] The route climbs the long couloir splitting the middle of the Devil's Kitchen Headwall: go up the snow and debris slope below the headwall into the couloir's entrance, then steep snow to the first ice step.
earlierWhy: why: Snow and ice couloir; approach glacier status not stated.

name: Devil's Kitchen Headwall (DKH) - Right Variation
text: [overview] It sits in the corner formed by the headwall and Steel Cliffs, and starts on moderate snow.
[detailed_rack] Kit varies with conditions: 2-3 pickets, ice screws.
[detailed_rack] Early June brought rotten ice-snow on the upper steepening, and firm snow lower, in the runnels.
[approach] The route is tucked into the angle where the headwall above the Devil's Kitchen runs into the Steel Cliffs, and begins on moderate snow.
earlierWhy: why: Moderate snow start; approach glacier status not stated.

name: Flying Buttress (DKH V3)
text: [overview] This variant has milder ice than the standard lines and finishes on the upper Wyeast route, with its steep snow crux and exposed gendarme.
[overview] Climb easy ice or moderate snow in the gully toward an apparent dead-end headwall.
[overview] Near its top, go right up an obvious snow ramp to the Wyeast ridge crest, then left along it past a small saddle where DKH V2 joins and a short traverse that may be the crux.
[overview] Moderate to steep, exposed snow follows, easing toward the summit.
[detailed_rack] Bring two tools, or one tool and an axe, plus pickets and a few ice screws if pitching.

name: Cascadian Route
text: [approach_variants] The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch.

[approach_variants] The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes..
[approach_variants] A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight.
[approach_variants] The first pitch begins at a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and you start just right of it.

[approach_variants] The negative marker is the strongest on this page, and it is about what lies further right: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the long snowfield, is unclimbed, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious.
[approach_variants] This route begins just right of a tiny snowpatch, not above a long one.
[approach_variants] If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.
[gear] two ropes for the Isella Glacier descent

[descent] Descend via the Isella Glacier, following a mostly continuous walkway of steep rock and mellow moraine at roughly two-thirds glacier height, then cross a notch in the south ridge back to base camp.

[descent_text] From the Southwest Summit, downclimb/traverse to the Isella Glacier and descend along an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then cross through a notch in the south ridge to regain the North Star-Bonanza col c
[seasonal_guidance] Mid-August to mid-September, when the loose west face is driest and the high camp approach is snow-free.
[seasonal_guidance] Snow lingers on the approach to the North Star-Bonanza col camp and meltwater loosens the already chossy west face..
[seasonal_guidance] Early-season snow and freezing nights on a loose Grade V face where retreat near the summit roofs is difficult..
[pro_tips] The descent via the Isella Glacier's 'walkway' at roughly two-thirds height is the key to avoiding the worst of the glacier.
earlierWhy: why: Descent crosses the Isella Glacier on rock and moraine near its margin; ascent has snowpatches.

name: Northeast Ridge (Sloan-Cadet Traverse)
text: [beta] The route follows the high ridge above timberline that runs between Sloan Peak and Cadet Peak, mixing Class 3 rock with snow and small glacier segments.

[beta] parties work around a corner with real exposure (sometimes protected with a short belay) then weave upward past a final short vertical rock tower, which can be avoided by scrambling up the gap between the tower and snow to its right.
[hazards] Snow and small glacier remnants on sections of the ridge.
[watch_out] Small glacier/snow segments are mixed in with the rock ridge and require care and appropriate gear
[gear] Ice axe (for snow/glacier segments)

[approach] Drop on grassy, rocky ground to the small tarn often called Cadet Lake, cross over Heineken Peak, and go down its steep grassy gullies to a low point near 5,600 ft above the remnant Mayflower Glacier.
[approach] The route starts there, on the ridge rising on the northeast side of Cadet Peak toward a small hanging glacier.
[descent_text] Cross the summit plateau and come down the standard route toward Glacier Basin.
[descent_text] Lower down a tunnel through the brush leads into Glacier Basin.
[descent_text] From the basin pick up the Glacier Basin trail, an old miners' path that is rough and overgrown, and follow it out toward Monte Cristo and the Barlow Pass road.
[pro_tips] The final short vertical rock tower below the summit can be avoided by scrambling up the gap between the tower and the snow to its right
earlierWhy: why: Mix of snow and small glacier remnants on the ridge; crevasse hazard unclear.

name: North Buttress Couloir
text: [approach_variants] Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine.
[approach_variants] Follow the moraine crest right (west, toward the glacier) and then drop into the couloir.
[approach_variants] Moat at the couloir entrance opens as the season progresses and can force a higher traverse in.
[approach_variants] Descent is over the back onto the Colchuck Glacier — soft afternoon snow there has been reported as slow and exhausting.
[approach_variants] The North Buttress Couloir rises directly out of the edge of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine — that relationship is the identification.
[approach_variants] Once inside, you are in a defined gully with walls, not on an open snow slope — if the ground stays open and fanned out you are still on the moraine apron.

[approach_variants] The moat at the entrance is the recurring problem and it changes the approach: when it has opened up, parties contour along the lateral moraine and traverse into the couloir higher rather than entering at its true base.
[approach_variants] If you cannot get from snow onto the couloir at the bottom, that traverse is the accepted workaround, not a sign you are in the wrong place.

[overview] The most direct couloir rising out of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine on Colchuck Peak's north side — a popular introduction to steep snow and easy mixed climbing, with conditions ranging from a straightforward snow slog to thin mixed rock-and-ice.
[beta] From the far side of Colchuck Lake, hike uphill to gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the large couloir at the edge of the Colchuck Glacier.
[beta] In winter and early season it is continuous snow the entire way;
[beta] The route can be climbed minimalist and fast, or fully protected with rock gear, pickets, and screws.
[beta] Descent is via the Colchuck Glacier route on the peak's far side.
[hazards] Occasional serious cornice at the couloir's top..
earlierWhy: why: Couloir rises from the Colchuck Glacier moraine; descent is over the glacier but crevasse hazard not stated.

name: Northeast Couloir
text: [seasonal_hazards] Late-spring systems bring new snow loading followed by rapid daytime warming.
[seasonal_hazards] avalanche, spindrift, rockfall, and a potentially corniced exit, all of which raise the consequence of any mistake.
[seasonal_hazards] Low - the approach crosses the lower Colchuck Glacier, which holds few crevasses;
[seasonal_hazards] the moat at the couloir's entrance is the gap to plan for, and it widens as the season goes on
[approach_variants] Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier.
[approach_variants] Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft.
[approach_variants] Do not continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route.
[approach_variants] Traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face.
[approach_variants] Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb;
[approach_variants] by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock.
[approach_variants] An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer.
[approach_variants] Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit.
[approach_variants] Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long.
[approach_variants] Walking up the Colchuck Glacier along its true-right margin you pass features in a fixed sequence, and this one is the second deep slot you meet, not the first.
earlierWhy: why: Approach crosses the lower Colchuck Glacier, described as few crevasses.
